name: Rosa Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Can you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I ride an electric moped around the city centre, takeaway and grocery orders, logged into three apps at once. Lunch is noodle bars and office salads, evenings are pizza and big grocery bags up to flats. I love the speed and knowing the one-way streets better than the satnav. What wears me out is rain, and restaurants that leave you standing at the counter for 15 minutes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you juggle three apps?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every morning I ask an AI assistant to compare last week's surge times across all three, and it tells me where to sit and when. I also buy broken mopeds cheap, strip them, and sell the parts online, which brings in maybe 300 a month. My husband Liam is a roofer, we married at our church two years ago, and we rent a small terraced house while we save for our own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that suits me. The tools I use already help me a bit, and nothing big changes. I can live with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the hype was overblown, but the useful bits are worth keeping. I'd probably post a little video for other riders about how I plan my surge times. People always ask in the riders' forum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I carry on building what I've got. Three apps, the parts business and my husband's roofing work make us steadier than most riders I know. The real pressures are rent and saving for a deposit, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep riding and grow the parts side, maybe two broken mopeds a month instead of one. I'd put the parts money straight into the house deposit account. And I'd keep using the AI to plan my shifts, because it pays for itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. Busy, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you keep the stripped mopeds?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In Liam's van space behind the house, under a tarp, which he grumbles about. He calls it my scrapyard. But he's proud of it really, he tells the lads on the roofs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How close are you to a deposit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About halfway, maybe two more years if nothing goes wrong. We want our own place before children, that's how we were both brought up. I'd rather wait and do it properly.

say: I'd say the **hype was overblown**, but the useful bits are worth keeping.
I'd post a **video for riders** on how I plan surge times.
think: Three apps, the **parts business** and Liam's roofing make us steadier than most.
The real pressures are **rent and the deposit**, not robots.
do: Grow the parts side to **two mopeds a month**.
Put the parts money into the **house deposit** account.
Keep using **AI to plan shifts** across the three apps.
S0.quote: Three apps, the parts business and my husband's roofing work make us steadier than most riders I know.
fieldNote: She runs her riding like a **small business**, with AI planning every morning.
Her **side income** from moped parts gives real security.
Traditional values show in wanting a **house before children**.
Calm fits: income is spread across several sources and the household feels secure.

steps.text: Keep riding across three apps in the city centre
Strip and sell two broken mopeds a month for parts
Put the parts money into the house deposit account
Use the AI assistant to compare surge times every morning

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This one is where the apps change the most, I think. The riding stays, but everything around it gets smarter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance for people who are quick on their feet. Online I'd tell other riders to learn the tools before the tools learn them. I'd be the annoying positive one in the forum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the apps would use AI to cut what they pay us, because they'll know exactly how little each rider will accept. That's already happening a bit. My answer is to spread my income even wider, so no single app owns me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use AI to run the parts business properly, write the listings, price them, answer buyers. I'd look at a small unit to fix mopeds for other riders, maybe sharing a rent of 400 a month with my friend Priya. I'd cut my riding hours down slowly as the repair side grows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the app pay. Excited about the shop, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't a repair shop a risk, with only a few months saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, but small. I wouldn't touch the house deposit, only the parts money. If it fails, I'm back on the moped full time and nobody's hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The riders who only use one app and don't speak the language well. They won't see the pay cuts coming, and they've got nothing else. Some of them send money home every week.

say: I'd call it a **chance** for people who are quick on their feet.
I'd tell riders to **learn the tools** before the tools learn them.
think: The apps will use AI to find **how little** each rider will accept.
My answer is to **spread my income** so no single app owns me.
do: Use AI to run the **parts business**: listings, prices and buyers.
Share a **small repair unit** with my friend Priya at 400 a month.
Cut **riding hours** slowly as the repair side grows.
feel: **Uneasy** about app pay and **excited** about the shop.
S1.quote: The apps would use AI to cut what they pay us, because they'll know exactly how little each rider will accept.
fieldNote: She sees AI mostly as a **pay-setting weapon** for the apps.
She takes **small, ring-fenced risks**, never touching the deposit.
She worries about **one-app riders** who send money home.
Uneasy: her own income is spread and holding, but app pay is shifting.

steps.text: Open a moped repair unit with Priya at 400 a month rent
Let AI write listings and answer buyers for the parts business
Fix other riders' mopeds for cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years to AGI, then robots by 2031. Right, so the delivery robots would be doing my streets in about five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who adapt will be fine and the people who wait will get hurt. I'd say it to my church friends and online, though I'd also say families need to stick together. I don't want the government running everything either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd lose the riding by 2031, maybe earlier, because the city centre is the easiest place for little delivery robots. The apps' thinking side, dispatch and support, would be all AI by 2028. Riding was never my forever job, but I'd expected another ten years of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd open the repair unit within six months, but aim it at fixing delivery robots and e-bikes, not just mopeds. I'd do an electrical repair course at night so I'm certified. And Liam and I would put the house plan on hold and keep the deposit as our safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with my sleeves rolled up. Two years is tight even for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would robot owners actually pay a small shop to fix their robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, honestly. Big firms might fix their own. But someone has to swap batteries and fix a wheel on a Tuesday night, and I'd want to be the person they ring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would putting the house on hold mean for children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the part that stings. We'd planned on children in three years, in our own house. I'd rather wait than raise a baby in a house we might lose.

say: I'd say people who **adapt** will be fine and those who wait will get hurt.
I'd also say **families** need to stick together, without the state running everything.
think: I'd **lose the riding** by 2031, since city streets suit delivery robots first.
I'd expected **another ten years** of riding, not five.
do: Open the **repair unit** within six months, aimed at robots and e-bikes.
Take an **electrical repair course** at night to get certified.
Put the **house plan on hold** and keep the deposit as a safety net.
S2.quote: Someone has to swap batteries and fix a wheel on a Tuesday night, and I'd want to be the person they ring.
fieldNote: She aims to **service the robots** that will replace her riding.
She admits the **uncertainty**: big firms might fix their own robots.
Delaying **children** is the real cost, and it stings.
Anxious: she expects to lose riding income soon but feels in control.

steps.text: Open the repair unit within six months for robots and e-bikes
Take a night course in electrical repair
Put the house purchase and children on hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years to AGI, robots around 2034. That's more like it. That's time to do it right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the one where nobody has an excuse, because you've got time. I'd tell younger riders to start learning a repair trade now. I'd be fairly loud about it online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd still lose the riding by 2034, but by then I'd want the repair shop paying both of us properly. Liam's roofing is safer than my riding, because roofs are awkward and dangerous. Between the two, I think we'd be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ride full time for three more years and pour the parts money into tools and a proper unit by 2029. I'd do the electrical course at a steady pace. And we'd still buy the house, maybe a year later than planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly focused. It feels like a project more than a threat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you bring Liam into the shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe in the winters, when roofing slows down. He's good with his hands but hates paperwork, so AI would do the paperwork for both of us. We'd call it Walsh and Walsh, my nan would love that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong with that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big apps could open their own repair hubs and undercut my repair shop. Or I could just be wrong about how fast it comes. I'd keep a bit of riding going as long as I can, just in case.

say: I'd say **nobody has an excuse** here, because there's time.
I'd tell younger riders to start a **repair trade** now.
think: I'd **lose the riding** by 2034, but want the shop paying both of us.
Liam's **roofing** is safer than my riding, because roofs are awkward.
do: Ride full time for **three more years**.
Put parts money into tools and a **proper unit by 2029**.
Buy the house about **a year later** than planned.
feel: **Uneasy**, but mostly **focused**, like a project rather than a threat.
S3.quote: The big apps could open their own repair hubs and undercut my repair shop.
fieldNote: She treats the change as a **project**, with a shop open by 2029.
Her husband's **roofing** gives the household a hands-on anchor.
She still names a real **risk**: apps opening their own repair hubs.
Uneasy: her riding goes, but the household income looks safe with time to build.

steps.text: Ride full time across three apps for three more years
Buy tools and rent a proper repair unit by 2029
Finish the electrical repair course at a steady pace

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, and robots around 2039. I'd be 40 with a decade to get ready. I'd take that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good problem to have, ten years notice. I'd tell people to treat it like a deadline at work, not like the end of the world. That's how my dad talked about anything big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think this one could be good for us. I'd have the house, the children, and a repair business that's been running for years before the robots hit the streets. The only worry is getting comfortable and missing the moment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the house in two years as planned and start the repair unit around 2030, once the children are a bit older. I'd keep using AI for everything on the business side. And I'd keep an eye on which robot makers sell into the city first, so I train on the right ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, actually. Even a bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned children. Would you work while they're small?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Part time, yes, the parts business from home. My mum would help, she's already offered. That's what family is for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything you'd regret in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not riding enough while it lasts, maybe. I do love the city at night on the moped. I'd miss that bit.

say: I'd say **ten years' notice** is a good problem to have.
I'd tell people to treat it like **a work deadline**, not the end of the world.
think: This one could be **good for us**, with a business running before the robots.
The only worry is **getting comfortable** and missing the moment.
do: Buy the **house in two years** as planned.
Start the **repair unit** around 2030, once the children are older.
Train on the **robot makers** that reach the city first.
S4.quote: I do love the city at night on the moped.
fieldNote: With ten years she sees the change as **good for her**.
Family comes first: **house and children** before the business.
She relies on her **mum's help**, not the state.
Calm fits: her plan turns the robots into customers rather than rivals.

steps.text: Buy a house with Liam in two years
Run the business paperwork with AI tools

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it would make me choose between the business and children, and I don't want to choose. What would help is cheap small business loans and short certified courses for repairing robots and e-bikes. Not handouts, just a fair start.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether riders get any say in what the robots replace. We know the streets better than anyone. A robot that needs fixing on my corner of the city is a job for someone who's ridden it for years.

headlineQuote: A robot that needs fixing on my corner of the city is a job for someone who's ridden it for years.
portrait: Rosa is a **27-year-old moped rider** doing takeaway and grocery orders across three apps.
She uses **AI** every morning to plan surge times and runs a **moped parts** side business.
She's married to Liam, a **roofer**, and they're saving for a house before children.
With **two years' warning** she's anxious and delays children to open a repair unit.
With ten years she's **calm**, planning to repair the robots that replace her riding.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it would force a choice between the business and **children**.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap small business loans** and short certified courses for repairing robots and e-bikes.
